newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivory Coast loosens used truck, bus import rules.
newsitem.headline: Ivory Coast loosens used truck, bus import rules.

text.p: Ivory Coast, enjoying a boom in car sales, has eased import restrictions on second-hand trucks and buses, a government statement said.
The statement, published in the government daily Fraternite Matin on Saturday after a cabinet meeting, said that trucks and buses would henceforth be treated the same way as private cars.
The government of the West African nation eased restrictions on second-hand car imports in April 1996.
"The change aims to sustain the economic recovery by injecting new life into the transport sector, an essential link in the national economy," the statement said.
It said that to ensure safety, arriving vehicles would have to be checked by Ivorian vehicle authority SICTA, which ensures all vehicles are roadworthy.
As with second-hand cars, they will be taxed at a rate of 41.62 percent.
SICTA figures show 13,597 second-hand cars were imported between April and December 1996.
The few that arrived before that were generally imported from Benin and Togo and Nigeria and subject to case-by-case commerce ministry approval and high customs duties.
New car sales have also risen -- to 4,748 in the year to September 1996, compared to 4,132 in the previous year.
Since then newspapers and billboards around the commercial capital Abidjan have been plastered with advertisements from car sales companies, many offering special offers.
Japan sold most new cars overall but France's Peugeot was the leading manufacturer, taking up to 30 percent of the market.
